newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Fresh fighting in Sierra Leone, civilians flee.
newsitem.headline: Fresh fighting in Sierra Leone, civilians flee.

text.p: Nigerian troops and soldiers loyal to Sierra Leone's military rulers fought with heavy weapons south of the capital Freetown on Sunday, sending civilians fleeing from their homes, witnesses said.

The cause of the clash at Djui, which began late on Saturday 15 miles (24 km) south-east of the city near Hastings airport, was not immediately clear, but a spokesman for the military junta installed after a May 25 coup blamed the Nigerians.

Residents said crossfire between Nigerian troops at a nearby base and the newly constituted People's Army -- made up of soldiers who backed the coup and their rebel allies -- had killed at least eight civilians.

"The Nigerians started attacking our men on the ground," the junta's spokesman, Allieu Kamara, told British Broadcasting Corporation radio. "The only thing that can bring this fight under control is for the international world to tell Nigeria to get out of our territory."
Nigerian commanders were unavailable for immediate comment.
One report said the fighting eased later in the day.

The two sides clashed last Wednesday at Lungi airport, across an estuary from the capital as members of the People's Army hunted for a clandestine radio station that has broadcast messages from ousted president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.
Nigeria, which had troops in the country under a defence pact before the coup, has since sent reinforcements as part of efforts to persuade the military junta to restore Kabbah to power.
Impoverished Sierra Leone's West African neighbours have agreed to try dialogue and economic sanctions as methods of persuasion, but have retained the military option.
Kabbah came to power in 1996 after multi-party elections ended four years of military rule. Rebels, who took up arms in 1991, rallied to the coup -- the third in five years.
